blocks.content: A caldera is a large basin-shaped depression formed when a volcano collapses into its emptied magma chamber.

rows: Built up around vent by ejected pyroclastic material and lava flows
Formed by collapse of the volcanic summit into an emptied magma chamber
Smaller diameter, typically less than 1 km
Extremely large basin, ranging from a few to tens of kilometers wide
Broad, steep-sided, flat-floored depression often holding a lake

items: Distinguish between Magma (molten rock beneath the Earth's surface) and Lava (molten rock erupted onto the surface).
Calderas are formed by structural collapse after explosive emptying of the magma chamber, not by outward blast alone.
Composite volcanoes frequently display parasitic cones along their slopes due to multiple fractured branch vents.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The magma chamber is a vast pool of liquid rock located beneath the Earth's crust that supplies volcanic eruptions.
The main vent acts as the primary vertical conduit through which magma travels upward to reach the surface.
A crater is a bowl-shaped depression surrounding the summit vent, whereas a caldera is a massive basin formed by structural collapse.
Parasitic or secondary cones form on the flanks of a volcano when branch vents direct magma away from the central pipe.
